items.followUp: Explain how the proton gradient in mitochondria is used to produce ATP.

rubric.why: Identifies the location and the electron-carrier system of the chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the electron transport chain is on the inner mitochondrial membrane and involves electron carriers (such as cytochromes).

rubric.why: Shows that reduced coenzymes supply electrons to the chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying NADH and/or FADH₂ as electron donors.

rubric.why: Connects proton movement through ATP synthase with ATP production.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the proton gradient drives ATP synthase to form ATP from ADP and phosphate.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen’s role at the end of the chain and the formation of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxygen accepts electrons (and hydrogen ions) to form water.

modelAnswer: The electron transport chain is present in the inner mitochondrial membrane and consists of a series of electron carriers, including cytochromes.
NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain; as electrons pass from carrier to carrier, energy is released.
This energy pumps hydrogen ions across the inner membrane, creating a proton gradient.

Hydrogen ions flow back through ATP synthase, which uses the energy to make ATP from ADP and phosphate; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.

items.followUp: Describe the roles of bile and pancreatic juice in digestion in the small intestine.

rubric.why: States both important actions of bile in the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that bile helps neutralize acidic chyme and emulsifies fats.

rubric.why: Gives the substrate and product of pancreatic amylase.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pancreatic amylase changes starch into maltose.

rubric.why: Gives the action of trypsin on proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that trypsin breaks proteins into peptides.

rubric.why: Gives the products of fat digestion by lipase.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

rubric.why: Describes completion of digestion by intestinal enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that intestinal enzymes complete digestion, producing simple sugars such as glucose and amino acids.

modelAnswer: Acidic food from the stomach enters the small intestine, where bile makes the contents alkaline and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Pancreatic amylase changes starch into maltose.
Pancreatic trypsin breaks proteins into peptides.
Pancreatic lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Enzymes in intestinal juice complete digestion: maltase changes maltose into glucose, while peptidases change peptides into amino acids.

items.followUp: Describe how white blood cells protect the body against pathogens.

rubric.why: Describes basic structural features of white blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that white blood cells are colourless and nucleated; mention of their irregular shape is also acceptable.

rubric.why: Identifies the main groups or representative types of white blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming granulocytes and agranulocytes, or appropriate examples from both groups.

rubric.why: Explains how some white blood cells destroy invading organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis.

rubric.why: Identifies antibody production as a defence function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that white blood cells, especially lymphocytes, produce antibodies and help provide immunity.

modelAnswer: White blood cells are colourless, nucleated cells and generally have an irregular shape.
They include granulocytes, such as neutrophils, and agranulocytes, such as lymphocytes and monocytes.
Some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis.
Lymphocytes produce antibodies, which help defend the body and provide immunity.

items.followUp: Define biotechnology and state one way it can benefit the economy.

rubric.why: Includes the economic aspect of the concept.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that bioeconomics concerns the economic importance or use of organisms or biological resources.

rubric.why: Connects biological resources with their use or value to people.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it considers the benefits, products or value organisms provide to humans.

modelAnswer: Bioeconomics is the study of the economic importance and value of organisms and biological resources.
It considers how these resources and their products can be used to benefit people and the economy.

items.followUp: Name one important medical work written by Ibn Sina and state its significance.

rubric.why: Identifies Ibn Sina by his other commonly used name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying Ibn Sina as Avicenna (or the commonly used spelling Avicena).

rubric.why: Names his major medical work or states its lasting significance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine) and/or noting that it served as an important medical textbook for centuries.

modelAnswer: Ibn Sina, also known as Avicenna, was a famous Muslim physician and scholar.
He wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine), which remained an important medical textbook for centuries.

items.followUp: List the main steps scientists use to investigate a biological problem.

rubric.why: Defines the scientific method as an organised way to investigate a problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a systematic or orderly method of solving or investigating a scientific problem.

rubric.why: Includes key stages used in the method.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming relevant stages such as observation, hypothesis, experimentation and conclusion.

modelAnswer: The scientific method is a systematic way of investigating and solving a scientific problem.
It involves making observations, forming a hypothesis, testing it by experiments and drawing a conclusion.

items.followUp: Compare xylem vessel elements with xylem tracheids.

rubric.why: Gives a distinguishing feature or function of sieve tube cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sieve tube cells are arranged end to end with perforated sieve plates and transport food through the phloem.

rubric.why: Gives a distinguishing feature or function of companion cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that companion cells are nucleated cells alongside sieve tubes and provide metabolic support or help with food transport.

modelAnswer: Sieve tube cells are elongated phloem cells joined end to end by perforated sieve plates; they transport food through the plant.
Companion cells are nucleated cells next to the sieve tubes; they support the sieve tubes and help maintain food transport.

items.followUp: Explain how the cell plate develops during cytokinesis in a plant cell.

rubric.why: Describes when and where the phragmoplast forms and identifies its basis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that during telophase microtubules or spindle fibres form a phragmoplast between the daughter nuclei.

rubric.why: Explains the phragmoplast’s role in forming the cell plate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the phragmoplast guides vesicles to the equator, where they fuse to form the cell plate.

modelAnswer: During telophase, microtubules between the daughter nuclei organise into a phragmoplast.
The phragmoplast guides Golgi-derived vesicles to the cell equator; the vesicles fuse to form the cell plate, which develops into a new cell wall.
